turns_text: [SEG0001] person_1 (PATIENT): Ag, sorry we're late. The robot by the Engen was out and then the bakkie wouldn't idle. Hectic morning, hey.
[SEG0002] person_2 (DOCTOR): Mm. Sit. What's the problem?
[SEG0003] person_1 (PATIENT): No real problem. My neighbour told me her husband landed in hospital with the pressure and she said I must come. I nearly didn't bother.
[SEG0004] person_3 (CAREGIVER): Doctor, I've been at the house these last weeks. He won't tell you straight, but that's why we're here.
[SEG0005] person_1 (PATIENT): Ja, alright. The ankles are a bit puffy and I'm passing water more often. It's nothing, really.
[SEG0006] person_2 (DOCTOR): How long for the ankles?
[SEG0007] person_1 (PATIENT): Two weeks. Well, actually, ja, two weeks. Doesn't even hurt.
[SEG0008] person_2 (DOCTOR): Both?
[SEG0009] person_1 (PATIENT): Ja, both. Left a tiny bit more. I still walk fine, so.
[SEG0010] person_2 (DOCTOR): At night, how many times?
[SEG0011] person_1 (PATIENT): Err, twice, sometimes three. I drink a lot of water, that's all it is.
[SEG0012] person_3 (CAREGIVER): His work boots don't do up by the afternoon. He just loosens them and carries on.
[SEG0013] person_2 (DOCTOR): Chest pain?
[SEG0014] person_1 (PATIENT): No.
[SEG0015] person_2 (DOCTOR): Short of breath, walking or lying flat?
[SEG0016] person_1 (PATIENT): No. Not at all.
[SEG0017] person_2 (DOCTOR): Headaches? Dizziness?
[SEG0018] person_1 (PATIENT): Uh, no. None of that.
[SEG0019] person_2 (DOCTOR): Tablets. Amlodipine and a water tablet. Doses?

[SEG0020] person_1 (PATIENT): Ja, for my high blood pressure. Amlodapine 10 milligrams in the morning, and the water one, hydrochlorothiazyde, twelve point five milligrams, also morning. I take them, every day.
[SEG0021] person_2 (DOCTOR): Any other medicine?
[SEG0022] person_1 (PATIENT): No. That's the lot.
[SEG0023] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pressure today is 162 over 98. What was home?
[SEG0024] person_1 (PATIENT): Yesterday morning, one thirty two over 84 on my machine. So home is fine. This clinic one always jumps, it means nothing.
[SEG0025] person_2 (DOCTOR): Right. Ankles.
[SEG0026] person_2 (DOCTOR): Pitting oedema both ankles, up to mid-shin. Pulses are present. Chest is clear, no crackles.
[SEG0027] person_2 (DOCTOR): Family. Diabetes, pressure, heart, stroke. Who has what?

[SEG0028] person_1 (PATIENT): My father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, my older brother is fine as far as I know. Another sister has pressure but no sugar, and my mother's brother had a stroke years back.
[SEG0029] person_2 (DOCTOR): Work, hours, food, exercise, drink?

[SEG0030] person_1 (PATIENT): I'm a forklift driver at a cold storage in City Deep, twelve hour shifts, six days. I eat pap and stew most nights, not much salad, I don't exercise apart from climbing on the forklift, and I have two or three beers on a Friday after the shift, that's it.

[SEG0031] person_2 (DOCTOR): Swelling like this on amlodipine is common. Could be the tablet, could be the salt, could be the veins, and I am not calling this heart failure. The night-time wees fit the water tablet. Leading thought is the amlodipine.

[SEG0032] person_2 (DOCTOR): Stop the amlodipine from today. I'll start losartan fifty milligrams once a day instead, for the pressure. Keep the hydrochlorothiazide at twelve point five milligrams in the morning.

[SEG0033] person_2 (DOCTOR): Because we're changing the pressure tablet and you're on a water tablet, I'll send bloods for kidney function and electrolytes today. If the ankles are not down in four weeks we might do a leg scan. Book back with me in four weeks either way.
[SEG0034] person_2 (DOCTOR): Cut the salt. Feet up in the evening. Don't stop the water tablet.
[SEG0035] person_1 (PATIENT): Ja, ja. If you say so. It's still nothing much, but we'll do the bloods.
[SEG0036] person_3 (CAREGIVER): I'll get him back here. And the salt stays in the cupboard, whether he likes it or not.

spec.situation: Patient on amlodipine and a water tablet with swollen ankles and passing urine often; blood pressure read at clinic and at home with different numbers; doctor changes one medicine.

traps.happens: In ONE long answer the patient lists several relatives and their conditions ('my father had diabetes in his fifties, mother did not, another sister has pressure but no sugar'), and in another long answer their job, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol.
traps.label_rule: Every relative with a stated condition is a separate family_history entry (relative, condition). Relatives said NOT to have a condition are not family_history entries. Occupation, hours, diet, exercise and alcohol/tobacco each become social_history entries as said (no inventions). Nothing from the doctor's questions is a fact.

traps.happens: The conversation OPENS with a remark, joke, apology for being late, small talk, or a trigger event (a relative's diagnosis, a neighbour's advice, the receptionist's note) BEFORE the real reason is stated. The patient states the real concern a few turns later.
traps.label_rule: chief_complaint is the real concern in a short phrase in the patient's wording (e.g. 'worried about diabetes', 'voice gets tired'). NOT the opening remark, the joke or the trigger (the relative's illness goes into family_history only if it is a relative's condition said as such).

features: doctor_thinks_aloud: the doctor lists possible causes or says what they will not conclude yet. Only record a clinical assessment if the doctor actually states a leading or differential impression; 'let's see what the tests say' is not an assessment.
hedged_plan: the doctor hedges ('we might do a scan if it does not settle', 'let's see in two weeks'). Conditional vs planned status must follow the words.

bad.reason: Pulses present is stated, but body site ankles is not specified.

omissions.text: Ankle swelling was bilateral, with the left slightly more than the right, and it was not painful.
Orthopnoea was specifically asked about and denied: no shortness of breath when lying flat.
The patient stated he takes both blood pressure medicines every day.
No other medicines apart from amlodipine and hydrochlorothiazide were being taken.
Home blood pressure reading was 132/84 on the patient's machine yesterday morning.
Family history also included mother without diabetes and older brother well as far as the patient knows.
The doctor explicitly said, 'I am not calling this heart failure.'
Bloods for kidney function and electrolytes were to be done today.
Follow-up was to book back with the doctor in four weeks either way, even if the ankle swelling improves.
